statement: Uphold te Tiriti in the Treaty of Waitangi Act and across government decision-making

summary.why: This party says that te Tiriti must be upheld as the fundamental document that the Treaty of Waitangi Act is based on. In its view, successive governments have consistently breached Te Tiriti, eroding the true partnership that was intended. Te Tiriti o Waitangi references have recently been weakened or stripped out of 19 acts of Parliament. And in government decision-making, iwi and hapū are often treated as advisors, rather than the partners which they are meant to be.
summary.how:
This party would amend the Treaty of Waitangi Act so Te Tiriti is the authoritative text. It would implement genuine Te Tiriti decision-making models across government, and ensure iwi and hapu are resourced to participate as partners.
It would increase resourcing for the Waitangi Tribunal and give it the power to make binding recommendations for the return of Crown and private land. 
It would facilitate the return of whenua outside of Treaty Settlements that was wrongfully alienated from tangata whenua, including a possible right-of-first-refusal process at point of sale. It would also reform the Treaty Settlements process to enable fair negotiations and just reparations without cessation of sovereignty.

statement: Support NZ made products, small business and sustainable industries

summary.why: This party says that small businesses are facing an economy that is stacked against them. Liquidations are the highest in almost 15 years and a lack of supermarket competition is squeezing shoppers and local suppliers. International corporates are flourishing while factories close and local businesses struggle. This party will work for an even playing field for local businesses and support sustainable low-carbon industries.
summary.how: This party would encourage consumer to support local by revitalising ‘Buy Kiwi Made’ and expanding country of origin labelling; commit government departments to buying more NZ goods and services; reform competition laws to create a fairer playing field for small businesses and consumers. It would foster sustainable, low carbon jobs in the ICT sector, particularly smaller firms. And it would invest in community-led regional development with a focus on sustainable building, regenerative agriculture, low-carbon infrastructure and iwi/hapū led economic activity.

statement: Better resource the agencies fighting anti-competitive practices

summary.why: This party says that small businesses are faced with a challenging landscape including a 15-year high in liquidations and a lack of supermarket competition which is squeezing local suppliers. Small businesses need an even playing field against international corporates where the profits go offshore.
summary.how: This party would reform competition laws to create a fairer playing field for small businesses and consumers. It would also increase the resources and powers of regulatory agencies investigating anti-competitive behaviour.

statement: Create a state-owned retirement village system and more support for seniors

summary.why: This party says that seniors have cared for us and many continue to do so during retirement. They should feel valued, connected and able to live with dignity. Seniors should have warm, accessible homes, and the community spaces and marae-based centres that support them should they need assistance. The says that, additionally, there should also be more support for the conditions and pay of aged care workers.
summary.how: This party would launch a long‑term seniors strategy that addresses kaumātua wellbeing, elder abuse, equitable incomes, and the creation of a state‑owned, not‑for‑profit retirement village system. It would boost funding for senior community spaces and activities, expand housing options such as papakāinga and address social housing waitlists for kaumātua. It would support warm, accessible, smaller home designs and back fair pay and conditions for aged care workers.

statement: Transfer responsibility for local elections to the Electoral Commission

summary.why: This party says that democratic engagement in local government is low, especially at turnout for local elections. Local government should have a mandate from communities and local elections should be consistent across the country, rather than being run by different private companies.
summary.how: This party would transfer responsibility of local elections to the Electoral Commission. Sixteen year olds would be allowed to vote in local elections and all councils would use a Single Transferable Vote (STV) system. To enhance democracy and community input, councils could use tools like citizens assemblies to make decisions, especially regarding reorganisation of council bodies.

statement: Ensure that fulfilling Te Tiriti and wellbeing goals is a core responsibility of local government

summary.why: This party says that tino rangatiratanga is often sidelined in council decision making. Local government shapes a lot of people's everyday life, and community wellbeing should be a priority.
summary.how: This party would reinforce the role of local government to give effect to Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and formally establish local councils as Te Tiriti partners. Councils would be allowed to reinstate Māori wards. Councils should also consider multiple sphere through the "four wellbeings" (social, economic, environmental and cultural) and take responsibility for more areas from central government, with appropriate resourcing.

statement: Reject the proposed rates cap and allow councils to use more funding tools

summary.why: This party says that councils have been loaded with new responsibilities like emergency management and tourist influxes, but not given enough money to carry out these responsibilities. To carry out their role in communities, councils should not have limits on rates set by central government. Instead they need appropriate resourcing from a range of tools.
summary.how: This party would reject the proposed rates cap where councils could only increase rates between 2 and 4 percent annually. Councils could set rates as they chose. Councils would also be allowed to use bed levies, congestion charging and charge GST on rates and other growth.

statement: Expand free mental health services to all communities

summary.why: This party says that people experiencing mental distress deserve access to care, no matter where they are. Social factors like the climate crisis, poverty and unemployment exacerbate the mental health crisis in NZ. Mental health services should be well funded and integrated into the public health system, not fragmented and requiring people to turn to private services which also have long waiting lists. Harmful practices, like seclusion, should be phased out so that care does not cause further harm
summary.how: This party would extend free mental health care to all communities, with more funding for community-specific mental health care. This includes youth services like Piki, Mana Ake and Youth One Stop Shops throughout Aotearoa. It also includes Asian Family Services and dedicated support for postnatal mental health. Mental health facilities would be further resourced so that the practice of seclusion could be phased out, replaced by community care models. Specific kaupapa Māori mental health and addiction programmes, including programmes focused on youth, would be funded as well.

statement: Implement suicide prevention recommendations, especially focused on youth

summary.why: This party says that all people in distress should be able to access support, especially as social factors like poverty, unemployment and climate change worsen mental health outcomes. Caring for those in distress and ensuring mental health workers are funded and resourced to avoid burnout will lead to better outcomes.
summary.how: This party would implement all the recommendations in Every Life Matters – He Tapu te Oranga o ia Tangata Suicide Prevention Strategy. It would also commit to further actions identified as part of a kaupapa Māori suicide prevention strategy, especially those aimed at reducing suicide among people younger than 24.

statement: Connect primary and secondary mental health care with clear referral pathways

summary.why: This party says that everyone deserves to access quality mental health care in the community where they live. Services should be culturally relevant and focused on the area of greatest need. With demand high and mental health workers burned out, making referral to secondary services clear, fast and consistent will lead to good outcomes.
summary.how: This party would link primary health and secondary mental health services with clear referral pathways in every health region. The focus would be on areas that have disproportionate need.

statement: Create an independently enforced Rental Warrant of Fitness

summary.why: This party says that a warm safe home should be a basic right, but much of NZ's housing is a source of misery and expense, while people who can afford to own their homes get richer. Housing should be affordable and healthy.
summary.how: This party would increase the stringency of the current Healthy Homes Standards for rental housing. It would also introduce a "Rental Warrant of Fitness" to certify that a house was appropriate to rent out, which would be independently certified.

statement: Increase public housing supply and housing support

summary.why: This party says that housing should be a basic right, not a "get rich quick" scheme only for those who can afford it. Building affordable, sustainable homes in the places where people want to live will focus on housing for homes, rather than housing as an investment.
summary.how: This party would increase public housing stock by building tens of thousands of new homes. It would fund papakāinga to be built on Māori land. People in need of emergency housing would be guaranteed "same-day" placement, and concepts like "housing first" and supported housing would be used for those in most need to support them to build a life in a stable home.

statement: Limit annual rent increases to 2 percent

summary.why: This party says that housing should be a basic right, not an investment that a lucky few can get rich from. Renting should be fixed so that healthy homes in places where people want to live are affordable.
summary.how: This party would limit annual rent increases to no more than 2 percent per year. The amount charged in rent for a new tenancy would be linked to what previous tenancies paid, so that there is not a jump in price between tenants.

statement: Implement a one-year pause on AI data centers

summary.why: This party says that AI data centres can currently be consented by councils with no community input. Overseas, data centres have had adverse effects on local water supplies and are high energy users, driving up power prices. The Datagrid data centre in Southland is expected to use 6 per cent of the country's electricity supply. This party says there needs to be more transparency and a chance for regulation to be developed.
summary.how: This party would call for a one-year moratorium on new AI data centres while proper rules are put in place to ensure there are benefits and don't unduly strain our resources. Solutions could include forcing centres to build their own energy or use closed loop water cooling systems, but currently there are no requirements for these under NZ rules.

sources.title: 'Call for a One Year Pause on Consenting New AI Data Centres', 26 July 2026 (accessed 18 August 2026)

statement: Encourage mixed-use areas and walkability in new housing developments

summary.why: This party says that a home is a place to build a life with loved ones. Building houses in existing urban areas will prevent cities from encroaching into rural areas, and mean homes are more sustainable for the next generation.
summary.how: This party would require councils to collaborate with communities, including mana whenua on decisions about new housing. Housing should be in mixed-use areas with shops and housing, within existing urban areas, and prioritise being able to walk around easily.

statement: Increase funding for food grants, food banks and other food security programmes

summary.why: This party says that NZ produces enough food to feed 40 million people, but somehow food prices are too high for many. Dismantling the supermarket duopoly alone is not enough to deliver food security, and demand for community solutions like food banks is immense. This party would offer more support to those building alternative models for food security, processing and distribution.
summary.how: This party would double the cap on food grants at the cost of $94-$100m annually. It would lift funding for regional food distribution hubs and community food providers from up to $8m to $25m a year and set up a $150m a year Fair Food Fund for community-led food security, such as food rescue programmes, marae and social supermarkets.

sources.title: 'Greens launch plan to break up the supermarket duopoly and bring down the price of food', 6 September 2026 (accessed 22 September 2026)
'Affordable food for all of us' (PDF), undated (accessed 22 September 2026)

statement: Make early childhood education free

summary.why: This party says that that early childhood education costs are a stress and barrier for many families, and that education should be a public good. This party says the competitive market in education has reduced trust, creativity and maintained exclusion.
summary.how: This party would first cap charges at $10 per day per child, on top of the 20 hour per week entitlement that is currently funded. This party would raise the funded entitlement to 35 hours a week by 2029.

sources.title: 'Green Budget: Early Childhood Education for Everyone ', 14 May 2025 (accessed 22 September 2026)

statement: Expand the school lunch program

summary.why: This party says that children learn better when they are well-fed and every child deserves healthy, delicious and locally prepared food.
summary.how: This party would restore Ka Ora, Ka Ako, the healthy school lunch programme, so lunches are provided by schools and local providers. Expand the school lunch programme to 400 more schools, providing lunches to 150,000 more schoolchildren. It would permanently fund the school lunch programme.

sources.title: 'Affordable food for all of us' (PDF), undated (accessed 22 September 2026)
'Green Party announces plan for free and nutritious school lunches', 20 August 2026 (accessed 20 September 2026)

statement: Repeal the Fast-track Approvals Act

summary.why: This party says that a healthy environment is important for healthy communities. It says mining projects approved by the fast-track act are destructive to wild environments.
summary.how: This party would repeal the Fast-track approvals act and revoke consents for new coal, gold or seabed mining projects.

statement: Restore the Ministry for the Environment

summary.why: This party says that that restoration and protection of the environment is important for the future and that a strong ministry is important for this.
summary.how: This party would restore the Ministry for the Environment, and increase resources for the Environmental Protection Authority to identify risks to the environment and to support compliance, monitoring and enforcement. It would also re-establish resources for the Community Environment Fund.

statement: Reset reforms to the curriculum and NCEA

summary.why: This party says that the current government's reforms to curriculums and assessments are rushed and ideological. This party believes education should foster curiosity, creativity and confidence, be grounded in Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and decisions should centre educators voices and expertise. This party says decisions are driven by standardisation and ranking reduces trust and creativity and re-enforces exclusion in education.
summary.how: This party would reset the current reforms and revert to the original direction of Te Mātaiaho, the New Zealand curriculum, and ensure reforms to qualifications follows reforms to the curriculum.

statement: Develop a long-term plan to support the teaching workforce

summary.why: This party says that education is vital for social cohesion and democracy and should be planned and funded to deliver this.
summary.how: This party would support the workforce to get fair wages and reach staffing levels that support quality teaching, and co-develop a long-term workforce plan with the sector.

statement: Regulate lobbying and party donations

summary.why: This party says that democracy should work for everyone, not just the wealthy. Capping donations and increasing the transparency around lobbying mean big money and professional lobbying can have less influence over politics.
summary.how: This party would bring in a package of reforms, including a public register for lobbying so meetings with politicians are on the record. Former ministers would have to wait two years before they can be employed by a lobbying group. A new bill would cap party donations at $30,000 per individuals, and companies will not be able to donate. Donors above $1000 would have to be named.

sources.title: 'Greens announce plans to get big money and influence out of politics', 22 September 2026 (accessed 22 September 2026)

statement: Expand access to learning support

summary.why: This party says that people with disabilities and diverse learners should be fully supported to learn, belong and thrive.
summary.how: This party would expand the criteria for access to learning support and establish a single agency for specialist supports for learners with health and disability needs. It would implement all actions in the Ministry for Educations 'Framework for Action: A Quality Education for All' strategy.

statement: Work towards creating a Māori Education Authority

summary.why: This party says that that education should be grounded in Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and Māori voices and communities should be central to decision making. It believes education should honour tino rangatiratanga and embrace te reo Māori and mātauranga Māori.
summary.how: This party would work towards a Māori Education Authority which governs and funds all Māori medium and Kaupapa Māori education. This party would support Māori communities to provide an education system that is driven by whānau needs and makes whakapapa-based decisions.

statement: Uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi in the new resource management system

summary.why: This party says that shared-decision making between the Government and tangata whenua is important to uphold Te Tiriti o Waitangi, and that this has been taken out of environmental laws.
summary.how: This party would secure the role of Te Tiriti in the resource management system and affirm the role of tangata whenua as shared decision-makers and kaitiaki (guardians). The party will also implement strong evidence-based limits for ecosystem health.

sources.title: 'Greens commit to undoing attacks on conservation and environment laws', 19 September 2026 (accessed 22 September 2026)

statement: Reverse changes to pay equity and fair pay agreements

summary.why: This party says that that women deserve to be paid fairly and the same as men for equal work. This party says changes made by the Government to pay equity shifted the goal posts for pay equity claims.
summary.how: This party would undo the current Government's changes to pay equity and resume pay equity claims, pay transparency measures and pay gap reporting.

statement: Improve endometriosis treatment

summary.why: This party says that that women face disparities in healthcare, especially for pelvic pain conditions and endometriosis.
summary.how: This party would work towards diagnosing and treating endometriosis faster. It would develop formal clinical guidelines for diagnosing and treating endometriosis, and fund specialist clinics for endometriosis across NZ.

statement: Create wrap-around services for new parents

summary.why: This party says that that single mothers are vulnerable to hardship and need more support.
summary.how: This party would fund a one-stop-shop service for new parents, providing pā harakeke wrap-around suppport for whānau during pregnancy, after birth, in early childhood, and throughout parenthood.  This is in addition to its policy to extent paid parental leave.

statement: Support kaupapa Māori and community based solutions to family and sexual violence

summary.why: This party says that that gender-based violence is increasing, and front-line organisations should be resourced to end family and and sexual violence in NZ.
summary.how: This party would will resource kaupapa Māori and community-led solutions to family and sexual violence. These solutions would be developed by groups that are disproportionately impacted by family and sexual violence, including women, Pasifika, rainbow and disabled communities.

statement: Amend the definition of consent to be free and voluntary

summary.why: This party says that that gender-based violence is increasing and women and gender minorities should be safe, respected and valued.
summary.how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to amend the definition of consent and affirm that consent must be free and voluntary, and can be withdrawn at any time.

statement: Criminalise coercive control

summary.why: This party says that that gender-based violence is increasing and women and gender minorities should be safe, respected and valued.
summary.how: This party would amend the Crimes Act to criminalise coercive control.

statement: Extend paid parental leave to 15 months

summary.why: This party says that women and families deserve to be safe and supported. Women deserve to get paid for their work, and compensated for time at home carrying out the essential work of caregiving.
summary.how: This party would increase paid parental leave to 15 months for the primary caregiver, and have additional ring-fenced leave for partners. This party would also increase payments.

statement: Fill empty stores by changing retail lease rules and addressing vacant buildings

summary.why: This party says that towns and cities need help to keep their centres vibrant. Empty shops are apparent on most main streets because of high rents set when the market was stronger. Many commercial leases don't allow for a rent review below the level set.
summary.how:
This party would ensure market rent reviews can lower rents as well as raise them. This will apply to both new and existing leases for businesses with a turnover of under $30m. 
It would also give councils the power to auction leases on shops that have been empty for more than a year, and a low-cost tribunal will be established for commercial lease disputes.

sources.title: 'Greens announce plan for city centre vibrancy ', 19 September 2026 (accessed 22 September 2026)

statement: Refuse to use AI for decisions on welfare payments

summary.why: This party says that the government's push for automated decision erroneously left tens of thousands of financially vulnerable people without funds.  Similar issues overseas have proven why decisions on who receives financial support should not be left to algorithms.
summary.how: This party would not use AI and automated decision making for welfare payment decisions such as cancelling, suspending, or reducing welfare payments, or imposing benefit sanctions.

sources.title: 'Green Party pledge to remove AI from welfare payment decisions', 11 September 2026 (accessed 16 September 2026)

statement: Recognise Palestine as a state and sanction Israel

summary.why: This party says that that NZ should be an independent voice against global atrocities, authoritarians, and imperialist ambitions. This party says most United Nations member states have already recognised Palestinian statehood.
summary.how: This party would recognise Palestine as a state and pass a bill drafted by this party to sanction Israel.

sources.title: ' Govt’s empty words do nothing to stop genocide in Gaza ', 11 August 2025 (accessed 23 September 2026)

statement: Rewrite foreign policy to oppose imperialism

summary.why: This party says that war and authoritarianism is rising globally, and NZ should be an independent voice for peace, freedom, democracy, and should speak out against nuclear weapons and American militarism. This party says foreign policy should challenge imperialism that creates chaos and hardship, and should always support countries facing conflicts and human rights abuses.
summary.how: This party would withdraw NZ from the Five Eyes security alliance and decline to participate in AUKUS, as part of efforts to step away from military and security frameworks with the United States. This party would rewrite NZ's foreign policy to stand against human rights abuses and focus on upholding peace and justice, and would have the Defence Force focus on climate change, humanitarian responses and environmental monitoring.

statement: Support sovereignty and independence in the Asia-Pacific

summary.why: This party says that that NZ should work with Pacific neighbours to create a greener, safer, and more just world. This party says NZ should be a world leader on issues of climate action, protection of nature and indigenous and human rights, and should work to uphold the international rule of law and collective obligations towards issues like climate change.
summary.how: This party would support Pacific sovereignty, independence, and oppose militarisation in the Pacific. This party would also support decolonisation and democracy movements globally, including those of indigenous peoples in Asia-Pacific region and work to urgently progress climate change initiatives through international institutions. It would support calls for West Papua to be independent of Indonesia, and for French-ruled Polynesian islands to be independent and call for an indigenous-led human rights investigation and a visit from the UN's Special Rapporteur on the Rights of Indigenous People.

statement: Increase democratic scrutiny of trade agreements

summary.why: This party says that that NZ should have an independent approach to foreign affairs and trade that focuses on climate action, nature protection, indigenous and human rights.
summary.how: This party would implement a suite of measures including increased democratic scrutiny of trade agreements, and enforceable recognition of Te Tiriti o Waitangi obligations, workers’ rights, human rights and climate commitments in trade agreements.

statement: Decriminalise cannabis for personal use

summary.why: This party says that harmful drug use must be treated first as a health issue, rather than a criminal justice issue. While there can be adverse consequences from drug use, not all drug use is abusive or problematic, and evidence indicates making substance use illegal makes it harder for people to seek help. In terms of drugs, cannabis causes far less harm than alcohol, methamphetamine, cocaine, or tobacco.
summary.how:
This party would regulate cannabis for legal personal use, with a legal age limit. Previous criminal convictions for these offences are removed from all records. Cultivation for personal use would generally be no longer illegal, and an evidence-based approach would be taken on which regulatory model best minimises harm. This includes improving drug-driving laws and providing education on the harmful effects of heavy or prolonged cannabis use.
Medicinal cannabis would be accessible and affordable for patients.

statement: Increase free public health services

summary.why: This party says that everyone should have reliable access to public healthcare, including during and after civil emergencies. This party says hospitals and GP clinics are stretched and over-capacity, and suffering from under-investment from successive Governments. It says private provider costs in healthcare are preventing people from seeking help early, causing health issues to escalate.
summary.how: This party would work towards free public primary healthcare and dental care, that can be accessed by everyone. They would increase focus on prevention and early screening, early diagnosis and treatment of non-communicable diseases, such as kidney disease, cancers, diabetes, cardiovascular and respiratory diseases. This party would fund the creation of mobile clinics for health care, mental health, diagnostic services and dental vans, for rural communities and during and after civil emergencies, including by-Māori, for-Māori community clinics. This party would also increase funding for data and digital infrastructure and capability in the health sector. This party would also regulate providers of private infrastructure and hold them to high standards of privacy.

statement: Simplify funding for Hauora Māori providers

summary.why: This party says that Hauora Māori and social service providers of healthcare are underfunded and restricted by contracts that are overly prescriptive. This party says Māori are underserved by the health system, and that progress to provide equitable healthcare has been undone. This party says kaupapa Māori health services should be supported to end health inequalities.
summary.how: This party would stop overly prescriptive Hauora service contracts. This party would simplify and improve funding arrangements for providers of health services for whānau, hapū iwi and hapori. They would commit to working with Iwi Māori partnership boards and Hauora Māori to do this.

statement: Improve wages and staffing for health providers

summary.why: This party says that that under-investment in health services has led to an understaffed hospital workforce and GP clinics that can't accept new enrollments. They say there are unsafe conditions for health workers and lengthy wait times. This party says everyone should be able to access timely healthcare from a supported workforce
summary.how: This party would ensure all health workers have fair wages. They would fund pay parity for primary care and hauora providers. This party would set safe staffing levels, to improve worker wellbeing and quality of care.

statement: Increase funding for Pharmac

summary.why: This party says that that Pharmac should invest in new health care devices and medicines so that treatment and quality of life for patients improves.
summary.how: This party would increase sustained funding for Pharmac.

statement: Expand the conditions that pharmacies can treat

summary.why: This party says that that pharmacists should help treat common health issues and should be encouraged to give appropriate medical advice. This party says they should be compensated fairly to do so.
summary.how: This party would Expand the Minor Health Conditions Service to help pharmacies treat common health issues, and update the Integrated community pharmacy services agreement to compensate pharmacists fairly.

statement: Support migrant workers to residency

summary.why: This party says that that people coming to NZ for work should have fair and achievable pathways to residence. The party says that migrant workers are not disposable, yet they face exploitation, are denied basic rights and are unfairly targeted by immigration compliance officers.
summary.how: This party would create new residency pathways for migrants who have settled in NZ long-term, including those whose visas have expired. This party would also allow migrant work visa holders to switch employers and would end the 12-month stand-down period requiring workers to leave the country between visas.

statement: Abolish acceptable standards of health requirements for migrants and refugees

summary.why: This party says that says that migrants and refugees with health conditions or disabilities are discriminated against by the acceptable standards of health requirements.
summary.how: This party would abolish the Acceptable Standards of Health requirements for visa applicants.

statement: Support families of migrants and refugees to get visas

summary.why: This party says that says that nobody should be unfairly separated from their families or communities. This party says people who flee war or persecution to seek asylum in New Zealand should be supported and treated with dignity.
summary.how: This party would clear the backlog for refugee family reunification, including resourcing Immigration New Zealand to clear the backlog of tier 1 and 2 family reunification categories and process asylum claims quickly. This party would restore birthright citizenship, expand work rights for partners, remove income barriers to supporting a parent visa, and stop detention and electronic monitoring of asylum seekers.

statement: Increase the refugee quota

summary.why: This party says that that people who fear for their life in their country, should be supported to seek a better life in NZ. They say people escaping war or persecution should be supported to rebuild their lives as part of our communities.
summary.how: This party would progressively increase the refugee quota to 5,000 by 2029. This party would also increase funding for refugee resettlement programmes and create a new humanitarian visa for family of New Zealanders in conflict zones.

statement: Create an immigration system based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi

summary.why: This party says migrants and refugees should be supported to rebuild their lives in NZ.
summary.how: This party would implement Māori aspirations for an immigration system based on Te Tiriti o Waitangi. It would develop resources and decision-making with iwi and hapū to strengthen traditional whanaungatanga connections. This party would also provide Te Tiriti education to new migrants and refugees.

statement: Increase benefit payments and improve standards for beneficaries

summary.why: This party says that everyone has a right to a liveable income that guarantees enough for food, safe housing and good quality of life. This party says the cost of living has got worse, and thousands of children go to bed hungry and families are struggling to pay rent or mortgages.
summary.how: This party would increase benefits to liveable rates and individualise benefit entitlements. This party would also abolish benefit sanctions. The party would reform the Social Security Act to uphold dignity of people seeking support and ensure everyone has a secure income, and implement a high-trust working model at work and income. This party would also overhaul recoverable assistance grants, write off existing debt to MSD and ban attachment orders against beneficiaries.

statement: Introduce a tax for net wealth over $10m

summary.why: This party says a wealth tax is part of a fairer tax system, that can reduce income inequality and ensure everyone has enough to live. This party says multi-millionaires pay $9 in tax for every $100 they make, while teachers pay $22 in tax for every $100 they make. This party says a wealth tax makes super-rich New Zealanders pay a fair share.
summary.how: This party would introduce a 2.5 percent tax on net wealth worth over $10m, with an exemption for the family home.

sources.title: 'Greens commit to tax the super-rich and large corporates fairly, cut income tax for 96% ', 21 June 2026 (accessed 23 September 2026)

statement: Expand ACC to cover income support and treatment

summary.why: This party says that that everyone deserves a livable income if they are unemployed, disabled, sick or a caregiver.
summary.how: This party would extend ACC to cover income support and treatment for injuries, disability and illness, regardless of origin.

statement: Strengthen working for families

summary.why: This party says that that families are struggling to pay rent or mortgages, to feed their children, or to warm their homes, as the cost of living has worsened. This party says that families should be looked after at every stage of life.
summary.how: This party would increase the working for families rate, reduce abatements and extend tax credits to families who are unemployed.

statement: Prioritise rehabilitation for convicted offenders

summary.why: This party says that rehabilitation is important to keep communities safe. It says current approaches to justice neglect rehabilitation, which causes more harm and hardship for communities.
summary.how: This party would resource evidence-based rehabilitation for anyone convicted of an offence. Tikanga based and restorative justice solutions, like Te Pae Oranga, would be available to anyone to access. This party would also improve community re-integration support for offenders leaving the criminal justice system, and would increase the Steps to Freedom grant to cover at least 30 years of inflation.

statement: Increase accountability in policing

summary.why: This party says that the justice system should be safe, equitable and fair. This party aims to meet the basic needs of communities in order to prevent crime happening in the first place.
summary.how: This party would require body cameras for frontline police and strengthen the powers of the Independent Police Conduct Authority. The party would also deliver de-escalation and trauma training for police, and increase resourcing for Māori Wardens and Pacific Wardens.

statement: End military-style academies for young offenders

summary.why: This party says that says the justice system should be fair and equitable. This party says people should not be punished for being poor, and communities are safer when young people have access to food, healthcare, education and have a safe home environment.
summary.how: This party would end military-style academies for young people and raise the age of criminal responsibility. This party would also ban young people being detained alongside adults. This party would expand access to specialist youth courts, including the Rangatahi and Pasifika Courts, Alcohol and Other Drug Treatment Court, and New Beginnings Court, so young people across NZ could access them.

statement: Improve accessibility to justice and legal assistance

summary.why: This party says that the justice system should be fair and equitable, and communities should be supported to prevent crime happening in the first place.
summary.how: This party would expand the district court initiative, Te Ao Marama, to all courts in New Zealand. This party would also extend legal aid and duty lawyers, better resource community law centres and make applications for protection and parenting orders free.

statement: Reduce restrictions on the decisions judges can make

summary.why: This party says that that laws restricting the decisions a judge can make about sentences have caused more harm and hardship. This party says bias and discrimination in the justice system should be addressed.
summary.how: This party would help enable judicial discretion in sentencing. This includes ending mandatory minimum sentences, life sentences, preventive detention, limits on sentence discounts, three strikes and limits on when home detention can be imposed instead of imprisonment.

statement: Extend hate speech laws

summary.why: This party says that that everyone deserves to live free from violence, harm and discrimination.
summary.how: This party would extend hate speech laws to cover religion, gender, disability and rainbow communities. This party would implement this alongside other recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Terrorist Attack on Christchurch Mosques on 15 March 2019.

statement: Implement the recommendations of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into the Terrorist Attack on Christchurch Mosques on 15 March 2019

summary.why: This party says that that everyone deserves to live free from violence, harm and discrimination.

statement: Implement recommendations of Royal Commission of Inquiry into Abuse in Care

summary.why: This party says that that the Royal Commission of Inquiry into abuse in care was a harrowing account of how society and the Government failed, and must change. The party says survivors have called for all 138 recommendations to be implemented.

statement: Ban alcohol advertising and sponsorship

summary.why: This party says that says it is important to take an evidenced, harm-reduction approach to alcohol and drugs.
summary.how: This party would would phase out all alcohol advertising and sponsorship, including at sporting and cultural events, and use funding from the alcohol levy to establish a national harm-reduction campaign.

statement: Enable licensing for psychedelic treatment

summary.why: This party says that the 'war on drugs' approach from 50 years ago has increased harm and addictions, and diverts money away from public health services. This party supports an evidence-based approach that prioritises people's health.
summary.how: This party would enable a licensing system for psychedelic treatment, and recognise taonga status of our native psylocibin (magic mushroom) species.

statement: Reduce nicotine availability and fund culturally responsive services to quit smoking and vaping

summary.why: This party says that that funding for addiction services should be increased, and NZ should take a harm-reduction approach to alcohol and drugs. This party believes young people should be protected from nicotine by stronger regulations for retailers.
summary.how: This party would phase out nicotine availability and fund culturally responsive vaping and smoking cessation services. This party would also implement stronger regulation and enforcement for nicotine retailers.

statement: Restore pay equity and negotiate a settlement for care workers

summary.why: This party says that the previous pay equity law better protected care and support workers who look after disabled people, older people and some of the most vulnerable people in New Zealand every day. However, this law was changed in 2025, and since then, these workers have been undervalued. This party believes a carer's pay should reflect the skill and responsibility their jobs demand.
summary.how: This party would restore the pay equity law to its pre-previous-government form. The party would also fund the settlement for the approximately 65,000 care and support workers whose claim was stopped after those changes were made to the law by passing legislation to settle the claim. The final settlement would be agreed through bargaining with the workers and their unions. This party estimates that this policy would cost $1.1 billion a year.

statement: Make public transport free for children and other specified people and cap fares at $2 for adults

It believes that years of underinvestment in public transport have left our cities harder to get around without a car. However, it says our cities have the potential to be accessible, vibrant and connected for locals and visitors. This will make it easier and more affordable for people to get where they need to go using cleaner modes of transport, also helping to cut greenhouse gas emissions.
summary.how: This party would make bus and train fares free for children, teenagers, students, apprentices, Community Service Card holders, and Total Mobility Users, and cap bus and train fares at $2 for adults.

statement: Protect 30% of the Hauraki Gulf by 2030

summary.why: This party says that everyone loves the Hauraki Gulf and we are supposed to protect and look after the things we love. This party wants to restore the marine ecosystem of the Gulf and ensure it is flourishing for generations to come.
summary.how: This party would commit to the Hauraki Gulf Forum's goal of protecting 30% of the Gulf by 2030, as part of its wider plan to protect at least 30% of New Zealand's oceans by reforming marine protected area legislation. It would also remove the ring-net fishing exemption from the Gulf's high protection areas immediately, through a Bill released in early October. Iwi and hapū would be supported to lead ocean protection in the Gulf. As part of its wider conservation policy, the party would also enable the Gulf’s fisheries to be managed according to the health of the entire ecosystem by reviewing the Quota Management System.

statement: Guarantee every 16-to 24-year-old who has been out of work for six months a pathway into education, training, or a new job

summary.why: This party says that youth unemployment is at nearly 15 per cent, roughly three times that of the wider working-age population, which is at an 11-year high. Yet there is so much work to be done in New Zealand. This party says it does not make sense, with nearly 100,000 young people not in employment, training or education. A long period without a job at the start of a working life also lowers a person’s wages for years afterwards.
summary.how: This party would establish the Jobs for Young People pilot programme, based on the successful Jobs for Nature model, to support new jobs in businesses, councils, iwi, non-profits or the public sector. It would also scale up funding of the Mayor's Taskforce for Jobs for all 67 councils, connecting young people with local businesses, community organisations, iwi and hapū. Lastly, it would make sure there is a national workforce strategy plan for young people.

statement: Ensure AI does not replace human judgement or democratic decision-making

summary.why: This party says that artificial intelligence should support human judgement, not replace it. Decisions that affect people's rights, welfare, health, education, employment, or access to public services must remain subject to meaningful human oversight and appeal.
summary.how: This party would require public registers of AI systems used by government agencies with full transparency around AI use, including where in policy processes it has been used, and where or how it has been used to inform decisions. The party would ensure people are held accountable for AI decisions and that everyone has a right to challenge AI-assisted decisions, and to opt out of being subject to AI-assisted decision- making.

statement: Protect data sovereignty

summary.why: This party says that data is a taonga (treasure). The party believes that New Zealanders, iwi, hapū, communities, and creators should retain meaningful control over how data about them is used. Language in particular is crucial to identity and culture, and must be protected from AI.
summary.how: This party would enforce explicit consent standards for AI training data, where appropriate remuneration must be provided for any Intellectual property used for training AI models. The party would ensure there are fines for any breaches, with the Privacy Commissioner given more power to enforce NZ's privacy laws. Government AI systems would be transparent, and there would be specific regulations requiring co-governance and co-development of Māori data and IP to protect Māori data sovereignty. Lastly, private information provided to the government and classified government will not be sent to third parties for model training.

statement: Place limits on AI data centres' use of water and electricity

summary.why: This party says that while AI seems like a virtual technology, it actually consumes large amounts of resources, taking up land, using water to cool servers and requiring electricity to power data centres. This party says that any data centres based in New Zealand would need to follow strict regulations to protect the environment.
summary.how: This party would require AI data centres to report on their environmental impact before being built. New facilities would be required to provide new renewable energy to cover their electricity use and their would be community consultation during the consenting process. To increase transparency, this party would require data centres to report their water use publicly.

summary.why: This party says that AI carries many risks, and can impact how information is understood. It says that news companies generate information and should be compensated by digital AI companies for how much information journalists generate ends up in AI summaries or responses.
summary.how: This party would update and pass the Fair Digital News Bargaining Bill, requiring AI companies pay local media outlets for data used in their AI summaries.

statement: Encourage the adoption of multiple types of AI

summary.why: This party says that AI companies can concentrate economic power, leading to bad outcomes for workers and individuals. These risks should be regulated by government.
summary.how: This party would encourage the use of public-interest and open-source AI models wherever possible, and mandate the use of multiple and interchangeable AI models to prevent vendor lock-in. It would encourage the use of NZ-based and NZ-focussed large language models, rather than relying on AI tools from overseas companies.

statement: Protect children and worker's rights in the use of AI

summary.why: This party says that AI can concentrate economic power and impact individuals and communities. Power should not be concentrated, and the use of AI should not be at the expense of children and worker's rights.
summary.how: This party would ensure children are not forced to use AI, especially at school, and broadly make sure that AI use around kids is in line with the UNCRC’s Joint Statement on Artificial Intelligence and the Rights of the Child. It would also require that workers are consulted about AI use in their workplace.

statement: Create an AI office and require transparent AI use

summary.why: This party says that people have a right to know when they are interacting with AI and how it is being used. AI content should always be clearly labelled so that people understand when they are using an AI model.
summary.how: This party would create labelling requirements for artificial intelligence, and audit algorithms for high-risk AI systems, so there is monitoring of AI use in the public sector. It would create an AI office within the department of prime minister and cabinet (DPMC) and aim to eventually establish an AI commission with independent powers to conduct audits assurance and education regarding AI use. This party would also collaborate with international best practice like the EU AI Act and build on NZ's work in the Christchurch Call to cooperate with like-minded countries regarding AI regulation and governance.

statement: Tax policy 'A tax system for all of us': wealth tax, capital acquisitions tax, higher tax on big corporates, bank levy, and income tax cuts for 96% of earners

summary.how: The 12-page tax plan (announced 21 June 2026). Revenue measures: a 2.5% tax on the net assets of the super-rich above $10 million (family homes exempt); a capital acquisitions tax on gifts and inheritances over $1 million (family farms and homes exempt); a 33% company tax rate for the largest 0.7% of companies while small and medium firms stay at 28%; a 0.06% levy on the liabilities of the four big banks; enforcing a 5% withholding tax on big tech profits sent offshore; and reversing the coalition's landlord interest-deductibility and bright-line changes. Income tax: a $10,000 tax-free threshold, new stepped brackets and a 45% rate above $160,000. The party's own Parliamentary-Library-based modelling puts the net gain at about $5.1-5.7 billion a year (2027/28-2030/31).

sources.title: A tax system for all of us — Contributing fairly to society (Tax policy 2026)

statement: 'Drink Swim Fish' freshwater and oceans policy

summary.how: A 4-page water policy (announced 6 July 2026) aimed at safe drinking water, swimmable rivers and healthier oceans: science-based national freshwater limits including lower nitrate limits, stronger wastewater-discharge rules, phasing out synthetic nitrogen fertiliser, phasing out bottom trawling and other destructive fishing, protecting at least 30% of oceans, and reviewing the fisheries quota system.

sources.title: Drink Swim Fish — Fixing the rules for fresh water and oceans

statement: 'Power for all of us' energy policy: Kiwipower, Warmer Kiwi Homes expansion, community energy and zero-interest solar loans

summary.how: The 12-page energy policy (announced 20 July 2026). It proposes 'Kiwipower', a publicly owned company to contract and build electricity firming; an expanded Warmer Kiwi Homes insulation/heating programme; $200m for community-owned energy; a government-backed Clean Energy Loans Scheme (modelled as zero-interest, tied to the property) for rooftop solar and other home energy upgrades; and other electricity-market changes. It includes four-year cost tables and says spending would be funded by the proposed super-rich tax.

sources.title: Power for all of us — Lower bills. Cleaner energy. Public ownership.

statement: Establish Kiwipower, a publicly owned electricity firming company

summary.how: A 6-page explainer for the proposed publicly owned firming company 'Kiwipower': it would contract access to existing hydro/thermal firming, invest in new renewable firming and storage (geothermal, biomass, batteries, small pumped hydro, demand response) and sell firming at fair prices to independent retailers and large users. Costed at $412.6m opex and $568m capex over 2027/28-2030/31, to be established by the end of 2027. (Image-only PDF; text transcribed by hand.)

summary.how: An 11-page policy (announced 9 August 2026) to recognise and resource marae as social and cultural infrastructure. statement: 'Safe, sovereign AI': regulate artificial intelligence for the public good

summary.how: An 8-page AI plan (announced 12 October 2026). It proposes rules so that AI does not replace human or democratic decision-making (no fully automated decisions with substantive effects in public services), protects data sovereignty, privacy and creators' work, operates within environmental limits (including controls on data centres), shares benefits rather than concentrating them, and is transparent and accountable.

statement: Pay students who need to complete work placements for their qualifications

summary.why: This party says that students completing important jobs, like midwifery, nursing, social work and teaching, are required to complete paid work hours to receive their qualifications. These students must show up for as much as 30 hours a week, making it difficult to hold down another job. This party says that as NZ needs more of the people completing these qualifications, people on work placements should be paid, and supported if they are completing placements in other parts of the country.
summary.how: This party would support students completing work placements for their study with a payment of $380 a week, on top of existing student loans or student allowances. Students who had to relocate for a placement (for example to a different region) would receive a one-off relocation payment of $1500.

statement: Provide $2000 to employers and apprentices to help with training

summary.why: This party says that for NZ's economy to get stronger, it needs a strong workforce. However, apprentice numbers are at a 15-year low. This party says that investing in people is a way to grow the workforce and economy and help apprentices to be supported in their chosen fields of work. Employers should also receive a financial incentive for supporting apprentices to complete their training.
summary.how: This party would give apprentices a $2000 equipment grant for buying tools, equipment or uniforms required for their qualification. Employers who take on apprentices who finish their qualifications would receive $2000 when the apprentice finishes training.

statement: Abolish the training wage

summary.why: This party says that apprentice numbers are at a 15 year low, even though the ork apprentices do is important and needed. Low pay and insecure work prevent people from entering the trades, this party says. It wants to abolish the training wage, which allows apprentices or people in training to be paid less than the minimum wage for work they complete.
summary.how: This party would abolish the training wage. All workers, regardless of training status, would be paid the minimum wage.

statement: Invest $30m in Māori and Pacific led trades training

summary.why: This party says that NZ needs more homes and renewable energy, and needs people who can do this work, such as builders nad electricians. However, apprentice numbers are at a 15-year low. It says that Māori and Pacific people face extra financial and structural barriers to completing training and this group should be supported specifically.
summary.how: This party would create a $30m funding lift each year for Māori and Pasifika-led trades training. This will include pastoral care, job matches and wraparound services for newly qualified workers.

statement: Protect at least 30 percent of the Hauraki Gulf by 2030

summary.why: This party says that it wants to protect at least 30 percent of NZ's oceans by 2030, including the Hauraki Gulf. It says this area around Auckland should be restored so biodiversity can flourish and people can swim and fish in the area.
summary.how: This party would commit to the goal of protecting at least 30 percent of the Hauraki Gulf by 2030. It would remove the ring-net fishing exemption from the Hauraki Gulf. statement: Aim to create a government surplus by 2029/30

summary.why: This party says that public investment is essential for economic development, productivity and resilience. This party says government investment can help grow NZ's economy and multiply impact later on. It says the government should increase revenue by creating a wealth tax, focusing on taxing capital and assets rather than productive work. Along with economic growth, this party says this plan will return the government to surplus while also creating better outcomes for New Zealanders.
summary.how: This party would return the government to surplus by 2029/30. It would do this by increasing the tax base, prioritising taxing capital (i.e. a wealth tax) rather than labour.

statement: Commit to future government operating allowances between $4.5bn to $4.7 bn

summary.why: This party says that the government can spend more money if it also creates a wider tax base, focused on taxing capital rather than assets. This party says the return to surplus should be delayed by a year because it is more important to focus on significantly increasing health funding. This party says that higher spending is a good investment for a government to make, along with changes to taxation.
summary.how: This party would commit to government operating allowances between $4.5 to $4.7bn for the forecast period between 2026 and 2029/30. It would invest at least $3bn of additional funding in the health system per year.
